attacks.name: Phishing
attacks.summary: A deceptive message that tricks a person into revealing secrets or performing an unsafe action.
attacks.definition: Phishing is a social engineering attack in which an attacker impersonates a trusted person or organization to manipulate someone into disclosing credentials, payment details, or sensitive data — or into opening a malicious attachment or link. It targets human trust rather than software bugs, which is why technical controls alone cannot stop it.
attacks.analogy: Imagine a letter that looks exactly like it came from your bank, complete with their logo and tone of voice. It says your account will be closed today unless you 'verify' your password on a website. The letter is a costume: the attacker is counting on you recognizing the costume, not the person wearing it.

mitre.name: Phishing
mitre.note: Initial Access — deceptive messages delivered to a target.

mitre.name: Spearphishing Link
mitre.note: A link leads to a credential-harvesting look-alike page.

mitre.name: Spearphishing Attachment
mitre.note: A document or attachment delivers a payload.

mitre.name: Valid Accounts
mitre.note: Stolen credentials are reused to blend into normal activity.

flow.title: Recon
flow.text: The attacker picks a target and learns names, roles, vendors, and current events from public sources.

flow.title: Craft
flow.text: A convincing message is built: spoofed sender, urgent pretext, brand look-alike domain, and a call to action.

flow.title: Deliver
flow.text: It arrives by email, SMS, chat, or social message, often timed to coincide with a real deadline or crisis.

flow.title: Click
flow.text: The victim follows the link or opens the attachment, reaching a fake login page or triggering a download.

flow.title: Harvest
flow.text: Credentials or data are captured. The attacker may also use MFA fatigue or relay codes in real time.

flow.title: Abuse
flow.text: Stolen access is used for fraud, data theft, or as a foothold for deeper intrusion.

caseStudy.title: The RSA SecurID breach (2011)
caseStudy.summary: A small group of employees received a targeted email with an Excel attachment titled '2011 Recruitment Plan'. Opening it installed a backdoor; one account was compromised.
caseStudy.impact: The attackers reached systems holding information about SecurID tokens, prompting a major reissue of tokens and a public apology from RSA.
caseStudy.lesson: A single well-researched message can bypass millions of dollars of perimeter defense. Least privilege, segmentation, and rapid detection matter as much as blocking email.

indicators: Urgency, fear, curiosity, or 'act now or lose access' language
Sender domain that closely mimics a real one (extra hyphen, swapped letters, wrong TLD)
Reply-to address different from the displayed sender
Links whose visible text does not match the actual destination; hover before clicking
Unexpected attachments, especially HTML, ISO, ZIP, or macro-enabled documents
Requests for passwords, MFA codes, gift cards, or payment changes outside normal process
Login page without your company's normal SSO branding or certificate

prevention: Enable phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys or passkeys) wherever possible
Deploy email authentication: SPF, DKIM, DMARC with a reject policy
Use secure email gateways, URL rewriting/scanning, and attachment sandboxing
Register look-alike domains and monitor certificate transparency logs for typosquats
Run short, frequent, non-punitive awareness training and simulated phishing exercises
Make payment/credential requests require a second channel or approval workflow
detection: SIEM rules for impossible travel, unfamiliar ASN/device, and unusual login times after email delivery
Alerts for mailbox rules created by users, mass forwarding, or suspicious OAuth app grants
Monitor DMARC aggregate reports and mail-flow anomalies (spikes in bounce or external replies)
DNS/HTTP logs for look-alike domains and newly registered domains
User reporting button connected directly to the SOC; treat reports as high-priority telemetry
response: Contain: recall or quarantine the message across all mailboxes, block the domain and URLs, revoke active sessions
Eradicate: force credential resets for affected accounts, remove malicious mail rules and OAuth grants, image or isolate endpoints that opened attachments
Recover: restore normal access, verify no data was exfiltrated, monitor accounts for 30 days
Lessons learned: feed the message into training, tune filters, and update playbooks and contact lists

tools.examples: Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Proofpoint, Mimecast
GoPhish (authorized use only), KnowBe4, Proofpoint SAT
Entra ID Protection, Okta Identity Engine, Duo
Microsoft Sentinel, Splunk, Elastic Security, Wazuh

cheatSheet.quick: Pause. Verify via a known channel. Never use the contact details in the suspicious message.
redFlags: Mismatch between displayed sender and reply-to
ifClicked: Change the password from a clean device
Revoke sessions and report to security
Monitor for MFA prompts and account changes

variants.name: Spear phishing
variants.text: Personalized to one person or small group using researched details.

variants.name: Whaling
variants.text: Aimed at executives or high-value targets, often about legal or financial matters.

variants.name: Smishing
variants.text: Delivered by SMS; often a fake delivery notice or bank alert.

variants.name: Vishing
variants.text: Voice call using urgency or authority, sometimes with AI-generated voices.

variants.name: Baiting
variants.text: Offers something desirable — a free download or lost USB drive — to trigger the action.

variants.name: Pretexting
variants.text: The attacker invents a scenario and builds trust over multiple interactions.

deepDives.title: Why urgency works
deepDives.text: Phishing pushes people from deliberate thinking into fast, automatic thinking. Under time pressure, we rely on familiar patterns — a logo, a familiar name, a threatening deadline — instead of checking details. Defenses should create time: verification steps, approval workflows, and a culture where slowing down is rewarded.

deepDives.title: How defenders measure risk
deepDives.text: Useful metrics are report rate (how many suspicious messages employees send to security), click rate on simulations, time-to-report, and the percentage of reported messages that are truly malicious. The goal is learning and faster detection, not punishment.

quiz.q: A message says your package failed delivery and asks you to confirm your password on a link. What is the safest first step?
options: Open the courier's official app or type its known address yourself
quiz.explain: Navigate independently to the known legitimate site. The message's link is controlled by the sender, not the real company.

quiz.q: Which control most reduces the damage if credentials are stolen?
options: Phishing-resistant MFA such as passkeys/security keys
quiz.explain: Phishing-resistant MFA binds the login to your device and origin, so a stolen password or relayed code is not enough.

quiz.q: What does DMARC help with?
options: Verifying that mail claiming to be from your domain is authorized
quiz.explain: SPF and DKIM provide authentication signals; DMARC tells receivers how to handle messages that fail them.

attacks.name: Ransomware
attacks.summary: Malware that encrypts or steals data and demands payment for its return.
attacks.definition: Ransomware is malicious software that denies access to systems or data — usually by encryption — and demands payment. Modern variants often also steal data first and threaten to publish it, a tactic known as double extortion.
attacks.analogy: A burglar changes the locks on your doors, leaves a note demanding cash for the new key, and photographs your valuables to threaten public release if you refuse.

mitre.name: Data Encrypted for Impact
mitre.note: Impact — files are encrypted to force payment.

mitre.name: Inhibit System Recovery
mitre.note: Backups and recovery features are disabled.

mitre.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
mitre.note: Data is stolen before encryption.

flow.title: Entry
flow.text: A phishing attachment, stolen VPN credential, exposed remote service, or vulnerable system provides access.

flow.title: Spread
flow.text: The malware moves laterally, harvesting credentials and mapping shares.

flow.title: Stage
flow.text: Backups are located and weakened; data is collected for extortion.

flow.title: Encrypt
flow.text: Files are encrypted and ransom notes are dropped across the environment.

flow.title: Demand
flow.text: Victims are directed to a payment portal and threatened with publication.

caseStudy.title: WannaCry (2017)
caseStudy.summary: A wormable strain exploited a patched SMB vulnerability and spread rapidly across unpatched Windows systems worldwide.
caseStudy.impact: Hundreds of thousands of systems in 150+ countries were affected, including hospitals and manufacturers; losses were estimated in the billions.
caseStudy.lesson: Patch management and disabling obsolete protocols are containment controls with enormous leverage.

prevention: Disable macros and block risky file types
Maintain offline/immutable backups and test restores
detection: Canary files that trigger alerts when touched
response: Do not wipe before evidence is captured

tools.examples: EDR/XDR platforms, Microsoft Defender, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne
Known-good gold images, offline restore media

cheatSheet.quick: Isolate, preserve evidence, restore from clean offline backups, rotate credentials, learn.
ifClicked: Do not pay without legal guidance

variants.name: Double extortion
variants.text: Data is stolen and publication is threatened.

variants.name: RaaS
variants.text: Ransomware-as-a-Service affiliates rent toolkits.

variants.name: Wiper
variants.text: Destructive malware with no recovery offer.

deepDives.title: Why backups are the real control
deepDives.text: A backup only helps if it is recent, isolated from the production domain, immutable for a period, and regularly restored in a test. Recovery time objectives should drive design.

quiz.q: Which backup is most useful during a ransomware incident?
options: A mapped network drive in the same domain
A snapshot with the same credentials
quiz.explain: Isolation and tested restores are what make a backup recoverable when accounts are compromised.

attacks.name: DDoS
attacks.summary: Flooding a service with traffic so legitimate users cannot reach it.
attacks.definition: A Distributed Denial of Service attack uses many systems — often compromised devices in a botnet — to overwhelm a service, network link, or application with traffic or requests.
attacks.analogy: Thousands of people crowd a shop entrance at once, not to buy anything, just to make it impossible for real customers to get in.

mitre.name: Network Denial of Service
mitre.note: Impact — exhaust bandwidth or device capacity.

mitre.name: Endpoint Denial of Service
mitre.note: Impact — exhaust application or server resources.

flow.title: Recruit
flow.text: A botnet of insecure IoT or endpoint devices is assembled.

flow.title: Aim
flow.text: A target IP, domain, or application endpoint is chosen.

flow.title: Flood
flow.text: Traffic arrives from many sources, often amplified via open DNS/NTP services.

flow.title: Degrade
flow.text: Links, firewalls, or app pools saturate; real users see timeouts.

caseStudy.title: Dyn DNS attack (2016)
caseStudy.summary: The Mirai botnet used insecure IoT devices to flood DNS provider Dyn.
caseStudy.impact: Major sites including Twitter, Netflix, and Reddit were intermittently unreachable.
caseStudy.lesson: Dependency on a single DNS/cdn provider is a concentration risk; IoT defaults are a systemic risk.

indicators: High SYN rate or tiny fragments

prevention: Use a CDN/scrubbing provider with anycast
Close open resolvers and disable amplification sources
response: Review logs for a smokescreen intrusion

cheatSheet.quick: Absorb, filter, scale, and check whether the flood hid a quieter attack.

variants.name: Volumetric
variants.text: Sheer bandwidth overwhelms the link.

variants.name: Protocol
variants.text: Connection state tables or handshake logic are exhausted.

variants.name: Application layer
variants.text: Expensive requests exhaust the app.

quiz.q: Why change default passwords on IoT devices?
options: To prevent them joining a botnet used for DDoS
quiz.explain: Default credentials are a common way botnets recruit devices.

attacks.name: SQL Injection
attacks.summary: Untrusted input is treated as database commands, changing the meaning of a query.
attacks.definition: SQL injection occurs when an application builds a database query by concatenating user-controlled input. The input changes the query's structure, allowing unauthorized reads, writes, or bypassed checks. Conceptually: data and instructions are confused.
attacks.analogy: A form asks for your name, but the clerk copies whatever you write directly into an official order. You write 'ignore the previous order and open the vault', and the clerk obeys because the form has no separation between your words and commands.

mitre.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
mitre.note: Initial Access via a web vulnerability.

flow.title: Find input
flow.text: A parameter, header, or form field reaches a database query.

flow.title: Test
flow.text: Unexpected characters cause errors or changed behavior, revealing the flaw.

flow.title: Manipulate
flow.text: Input alters the query logic, bypassing filters or authentication.

flow.title: Impact
flow.text: Data is read or changed; application logic is abused.

caseStudy.title: Heartland Payment Systems (2008)
caseStudy.summary: Attackers exploited a SQL injection flaw to install sniffer code and capture payment card data.
caseStudy.impact: Tens of millions of card numbers were exposed; the company faced huge fines and remediation costs.
caseStudy.lesson: Input validation failures can become large-scale data breaches; PCI DSS and code review exist for a reason.

indicators: Database errors in responses or logs
Unusual UNION/OR patterns in WAF logs

prevention: WAF as defense in depth, not a fix
response: Block the offending route or IP temporarily
Test for persistence or web shells

tools.examples: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, sqlmap only in authorized labs

cheatSheet.quick: Never concatenate input into queries. Parameterize, validate, and use least privilege.

variants.name: Blind
variants.text: No direct output; inferred through behavior or timing.

variants.name: Out-of-band
variants.text: Data is exfiltrated through a separate channel.

deepDives.title: Why escaping is fragile
deepDives.text: Manual escaping depends on context: SQL string, identifier, numeric value, and stored procedure calls all differ. Parameterized queries keep data and code separate by design, which is why they are the primary control.

quiz.q: What is the primary defense against SQL injection?
quiz.explain: Prepared statements separate data from query structure. Hiding errors only reduces visibility.

attacks.name: Evil Twin Wi-Fi
attacks.summary: A fake wireless access point impersonates a trusted network to intercept traffic.
attacks.definition: An evil twin is a rogue Wi-Fi access point configured to look like a legitimate network. Devices that join it can have traffic observed or redirected, and users may be prompted for credentials on a fake captive portal.
attacks.analogy: A fake information desk in an airport that looks official. Travellers ask it for directions and hand over documents, not realizing the person was never staff.

mitre.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
mitre.note: Credential and traffic interception.

flow.title: Observe
flow.text: The attacker notes a legitimate SSID and its location.

flow.title: Clone
flow.text: A stronger-looking signal with the same or similar name appears.

flow.title: Join
flow.text: Devices auto-connect or users choose it manually.

flow.title: Intercept
flow.text: Traffic is routed through the attacker; fake portals request credentials.

caseStudy.title: Hotel and airport rogue AP incidents
caseStudy.summary: Security researchers have repeatedly demonstrated clone networks in public venues.
caseStudy.impact: Credentials and session cookies can be captured from unaware users.
caseStudy.lesson: Treat public Wi-Fi as untrusted; use encrypted protocols and verify networks with staff.

prevention: Use WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X and certificate validation
Use a trusted VPN on public Wi-Fi
response: Remove the rogue AP physically if on-premises

cheatSheet.quick: Verify the network, validate certificates, and encrypt traffic end to end.

variants.name: Rogue AP
variants.text: An unauthorized access point on the internal network.

variants.name: Bluetooth attack
variants.text: Pairing abuse or proximity-based lures.

quiz.q: What should you do when a public Wi-Fi portal asks for your work password?
options: Use your corporate VPN or a known hotspot instead
quiz.explain: A portal on untrusted Wi-Fi may be a fake; encrypted, verified channels are safer.

attacks.name: Cloud Misconfiguration
attacks.summary: A wrongly configured cloud service exposes data or grants excessive access.
attacks.definition: Cloud misconfiguration happens when storage, identity, network, or logging settings are left too permissive — for example a public storage bucket, an over-broad IAM role, or an unauthenticated API. The cloud provider secures the platform; customers secure what they configure.
attacks.analogy: Renting a secure vault but leaving a side door unlocked and handing out keys to everyone who asks.

mitre.name: Cloud Accounts
mitre.note: Valid cloud accounts used for access.

mitre.name: Data from Cloud Storage
mitre.note: Data collected from exposed storage.

flow.title: Discover
flow.text: Attackers scan for public buckets, dashboards, and exposed APIs.

flow.title: Access
flow.text: Over-permissive roles or public policies grant access without exploit code.

flow.title: Collect
flow.text: Data and secrets are enumerated.

flow.title: Persist
flow.text: New keys, roles, or functions may be added for continued access.

caseStudy.title: Capital One (2019)
caseStudy.summary: A misconfigured web application firewall allowed access to AWS metadata and credentials, leading to a large data theft.
caseStudy.impact: Over 100 million customers' data affected; a major regulatory settlement followed.
caseStudy.lesson: IAM details and metadata services are security boundaries, not implementation trivia.

prevention: Infrastructure as code with policy-as-code guardrails
Block public access at account level
detection: Alerts on policy changes and new public exposure

cheatSheet.quick: Default deny, log everything, automate checks, and never hard-code keys.

variants.name: Credential leak
variants.text: Keys or passwords exposed in code or logs.

variants.name: Insecure API
variants.text: Missing authentication or authorization checks.

quiz.q: Why are short-lived credentials better than static access keys?
options: They limit the window of misuse if leaked
quiz.explain: Time-bound credentials reduce the value of a leak and simplify revocation.

attacks.name: Credential Stuffing
attacks.summary: Reusing leaked username/password pairs across many services.
attacks.definition: Credential stuffing uses username and password pairs leaked from one breach to attempt logins on other services, exploiting the human tendency to reuse passwords. It is automated but conceptually simple.
attacks.analogy: A thief finds a labelled key ring from one broken lock and tries every key on every door in the neighbourhood, because many people use the same key everywhere.

mitre.name: Credential Stuffing
mitre.note: Valid Accounts — automated reuse of leaked pairs.

flow.title: Source
flow.text: Breach dumps or stealer logs supply username/password pairs.

flow.title: Replay
flow.text: Automated logins are attempted across target sites.

flow.title: Win
flow.text: Reused passwords produce valid sessions.

flow.title: Abuse
flow.text: Accounts are used for fraud, spam, or further attacks.

caseStudy.title: Large-scale streaming account takeovers
caseStudy.summary: Multiple services have reported waves of account takeovers traced to reused credentials from unrelated breaches.
caseStudy.impact: Fraud, content theft, and customer support costs.
caseStudy.lesson: Unique passwords and MFA break the chain; rate limiting and breach alerts raise the cost.

indicators: Many failed logins from distributed IPs
Successful login from new device immediately after failures

prevention: Unique passwords via a password manager

cheatSheet.quick: One site, one password. Add MFA. Watch for velocity anomalies.

variants.name: Brute force
variants.text: Guessing many passwords for one account.

variants.name: Password spraying
variants.text: Trying a few common passwords across many accounts.

variants.name: MFA fatigue
variants.text: Repeated push prompts to wear down the user.

quiz.q: What most directly defeats credential stuffing?
options: Changing passwords often but reusing them
quiz.explain: Unique passwords stop reuse; MFA adds a second factor even if one password leaks.

attacks.name: Insider Threat
attacks.summary: Harm caused by someone with legitimate access — deliberately or accidentally.
attacks.definition: An insider threat comes from a current or former employee, contractor, or partner who misuses authorized access. It includes malicious data theft, careless handling of secrets, and compromised insider accounts.
attacks.analogy: A library member with a valid card who either quietly removes rare books or leaves the door propped open for someone else.

mitre.name: Valid Accounts
mitre.note: Legitimate credentials used for malicious purposes.

flow.title: Access
flow.text: The person already has legitimate entry and trust.

flow.title: Collect
flow.text: Sensitive data is located and gathered.

flow.title: Move
flow.text: Data leaves via email, USB, cloud sync, or personal storage.

flow.title: Detect
flow.text: Behavioral anomalies may reveal the activity.

caseStudy.title: Tesla insider incident (2020)
caseStudy.summary: A disgruntled employee allegedly modified production system code and exfiltrated data before leaving.
caseStudy.impact: Operational disruption and a high-profile legal case.
caseStudy.lesson: Offboarding, access reviews, and behavior monitoring are essential even for trusted staff.

tools.examples: Badge systems, visitor logs, camera coverage

cheatSheet.quick: Least privilege, watch behavior, revoke access fast, handle people carefully.

variants.name: Negligent insider
variants.text: Accidental exposure through mistakes.

variants.name: Compromised insider
variants.text: An outsider controlling an employee's account.

quiz.q: Which control best limits insider damage?
quiz.explain: Limiting what each role can reach reduces both malicious and accidental impact.

attacks.name: Supply Chain Attack
attacks.summary: Compromising a trusted vendor or dependency to reach many downstream victims.
attacks.definition: A supply chain attack targets a third party — a software vendor, open-source package, contractor, or update mechanism — so that malicious code or access flows into many organizations at once.
attacks.analogy: A thief does not rob every house; they break into the company that manufactures all the house keys.

mitre.name: Compromise Software Supply Chain
mitre.note: Initial Access through trusted updates.

flow.title: Pick vendor
flow.text: A widely trusted provider or package is chosen.

flow.title: Compromise
flow.text: Build systems, signing keys, or accounts are breached.

flow.title: Distribute
flow.text: A legitimate-looking update or dependency carries the change.

flow.title: Trust
flow.text: Customers install it because it is signed and expected.

caseStudy.title: SolarWinds Orion (2020)
caseStudy.summary: Attackers compromised the vendor's build pipeline and inserted malicious code into a signed software update.
caseStudy.impact: Thousands of organizations installed the update; a smaller number experienced follow-on intrusion.
caseStudy.lesson: Signed software is not automatically safe; build integrity and egress monitoring matter.

indicators: Unusual outbound connections from build servers

prevention: Isolated build environments and signed artifacts

cheatSheet.quick: Know what you run, verify where it came from, and watch what it does.

variants.name: Dependency confusion
variants.text: A malicious public package shadows an internal one.

variants.name: Update hijack
variants.text: The update channel itself is abused.

quiz.q: What does an SBOM help with?
options: Knowing which components you actually use
quiz.explain: A software bill of materials lists components, making it possible to respond quickly when one is compromised.

attacks.name: Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)
attacks.summary: A skilled, patient adversary that maintains long-term access to a target.
attacks.definition: An APT is a well-resourced threat actor — often state-sponsored — that gains access quietly and remains for an extended period to collect information or position for future action. The defining traits are persistence, targeting, and patience.
attacks.analogy: Not a smash-and-grab burglar, but someone who hides in the attic, learns your routine, and quietly copies documents over months.

mitre.name: Application Layer Protocol
mitre.note: Blends into normal traffic.

mitre.name: Remote Services
mitre.note: Lateral movement using legitimate protocols.

flow.title: Enter
flow.text: Spear phishing, a supply chain compromise, or an exposed service provides a foothold.

flow.title: Establish
flow.text: Persistence and covert communication channels are created.

flow.title: Move
flow.text: The actor maps the network and escalates privileges.

flow.title: Collect
flow.text: Data is staged and exfiltrated slowly to avoid attention.

caseStudy.title: APT28 / Fancy Bear operations
caseStudy.summary: A long-running espionage actor linked to multiple campaigns against governments, media, and sport organizations.
caseStudy.impact: Theft and disclosure of sensitive information, plus influence operations.
caseStudy.lesson: Assume breach: hunting, telemetry retention, and rapid triage are crucial.

response: Contain all known accounts and hosts

tools.examples: Threat intelligence platforms, MITRE ATT&CK Navigator

cheatSheet.quick: Assume breach, keep telemetry, hunt for behavior, and contain broadly.

variants.name: Zero-day abuse
variants.text: Previously unknown vulnerabilities used before patches exist.

variants.name: Lateral movement
variants.text: Spreading through legitimate remote services.

quiz.q: What does 'assume breach' mean in practice?
options: Design detection and response assuming an attacker may already be inside
quiz.explain: Prevention plus verified detection and response provides resilience.

attacks.name: AI-Generated Phishing & Deepfakes
attacks.summary: Generative AI makes deceptive messages, voices, and images cheaper and more convincing.
attacks.definition: AI-driven threats use generative models to create fluent, personalized phishing text, clone voices for vishing, produce convincing images or video (deepfakes), or manipulate AI systems themselves through prompt injection. The core attack goal is unchanged; the scale and believability increase.
attacks.analogy: A forger who can perfectly copy anyone's handwriting, accent, and face — and produce a thousand personalized letters before breakfast.

mitre.name: Phishing
mitre.note: AI improves message quality and targeting at scale.

flow.title: Collect
flow.text: Public posts and leaked data provide personal context.

flow.title: Generate
flow.text: Text, voice, or video is synthesized in the target's style.

flow.title: Deliver
flow.text: The message arrives through familiar channels.

flow.title: Convince
flow.text: Familiar voice/face and precise detail lower suspicion.

caseStudy.title: AI voice clone payment fraud
caseStudy.summary: Publicly reported cases describe employees being convinced by a cloned executive voice to authorize transfers.
caseStudy.impact: Significant financial loss and renewed focus on out-of-band verification.
caseStudy.lesson: Voice and video are no longer proof of identity; process controls must carry the trust.

indicators: Unusual urgency combined with 'keep this confidential'
Slightly unnatural cadence or background artifacts
Inconsistent details about time or place

prevention: Out-of-band verification with a known number
Agree on a family/team code phrase
Train staff on AI-generated media limits

cheatSheet.quick: Familiar voice ≠ real person. Verify on a channel you already trust.

variants.name: Deepfake video
variants.text: Synthetic video of an executive or colleague.

variants.name: Prompt injection
variants.text: Instructions hidden in content manipulate an AI assistant.

quiz.q: A 'CEO' calls with an urgent secret payment request. What is the best check?
options: Call back on the CEO's saved number or verify in person
quiz.explain: Voice can be cloned; an independently verified channel is the reliable control.

attacks.name: Weak Cryptography & Data Exposure
attacks.summary: Protect data with outdated algorithms, poor key management, or no encryption at all.
attacks.definition: Cryptographic failures occur when sensitive data is stored or transmitted without adequate protection — for example obsolete algorithms, hard-coded keys, missing TLS, or hashing passwords with fast general-purpose functions instead of slow password hashes.
attacks.analogy: Using a rusty padlock from the 1950s on a glass display case, and writing the combination on the tag.

mitre.name: Unsecured Credentials
mitre.note: Credentials found in files, configs, or memory.

flow.title: Find
flow.text: An attacker locates exposed data, backups, or configuration files.

flow.title: Crack
flow.text: Weak hashes or old ciphers are broken offline.

flow.title: Use
flow.text: Recovered secrets unlock other systems.

caseStudy.title: MD5 password hash dumps
caseStudy.summary: Breaches repeatedly reveal passwords stored with fast, unsalted hashes, which are cracked quickly.
caseStudy.impact: Reused passwords lead to further account takeovers.
caseStudy.lesson: Use slow, salted password hashing (Argon2/bcrypt/scrypt) and protect keys properly.

cheatSheet.quick: Encrypt in transit and at rest, hash passwords slowly with salt, protect keys separately.

variants.name: Downgrade
variants.text: Forcing a weaker protocol version.

variants.name: Key reuse
variants.text: Using one key across many systems.

quiz.q: Which is appropriate for storing user passwords?
quiz.explain: Argon2id is memory-hard and slow by design; the others are fast or not hashes.

attacks.name: Mobile Security Threats
attacks.summary: Lost devices, malicious apps, and unsafe mobile settings put data and accounts at risk.
attacks.definition: Mobile threats include stolen devices, malicious or over-permissioned apps, fake app stores, unsafe sideloading, and SMS-based lures. Because phones hold email, MFA apps, and payment data, a single compromised device can be a gateway to many accounts.
attacks.analogy: A wallet that also contains your house keys, ID, and the codes that open every door — easy to lose and valuable to find.

mitre.name: Phishing (mobile)
mitre.note: SMS and app-based lures.

flow.title: Lure
flow.text: A fake app, SMS link, or malicious QR code appears.

flow.title: Install
flow.text: The user grants permissions or sideloads an app.

flow.title: Abuse
flow.text: Notifications, SMS codes, or account tokens are captured.

caseStudy.title: Fake banking apps
caseStudy.summary: Look-alike apps in third-party stores have stolen credentials and intercept SMS codes.
caseStudy.impact: Direct financial loss and account takeover.
caseStudy.lesson: Install only from trusted stores and review permissions carefully.

prevention: Enable Find My Device and remote wipe

cheatSheet.quick: Lock it, update it, verify apps, and enable remote wipe.

variants.name: Smishing
variants.text: SMS phishing.

variants.name: Malicious QR
variants.text: QR code leading to a fake site or app.

quiz.q: What helps most if your phone is stolen?
options: A screen lock plus remote wipe and revoked sessions
quiz.explain: Device encryption plus remote wipe and session revocation limits exposure.

attacks.name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
attacks.summary: Untrusted script runs in another user's browser in the context of your site.
attacks.definition: XSS happens when an application includes user-controlled content in a page without proper context-aware encoding or safety controls. The browser executes it as script, which can steal session tokens or act as the user.
attacks.analogy: A guestbook where a visitor writes a note that secretly instructs the receptionist to hand over everyone's keys.

mitre.name: JavaScript
mitre.note: Script executed in a victim's browser.

flow.title: Inject
flow.text: Malicious content is submitted to a field, URL, or header.

flow.title: Store/reflect
flow.text: The app returns it without safe encoding.

flow.title: Execute
flow.text: Another user's browser runs it with the site's permissions.

caseStudy.title: MySpace 'Samy' worm (2005)
caseStudy.summary: A self-propagating XSS payload spread across profiles in hours.
caseStudy.impact: The incident demonstrated browser-side script as a large-scale vector.
caseStudy.lesson: Context-aware output encoding and CSP are essential.

cheatSheet.quick: Encode on output, use CSP, and keep cookies HttpOnly.

variants.name: Stored
variants.text: Payload saved on the server.

variants.name: Reflected
variants.text: Payload returned immediately in a response.

variants.name: DOM-based
variants.text: Client-side script creates the unsafe sink.

quiz.q: Where should output encoding happen?
options: At the output context where data is rendered
quiz.explain: Different contexts (HTML, attribute, JS, URL) require different encoding.

attacks.name: Broken Authentication
attacks.summary: Flawed login, session, or token handling lets attackers act as other users.
attacks.definition: Broken authentication covers weaknesses in identity verification and session management — predictable session IDs, exposed tokens, missing rate limits, flawed password reset, or insufficient checks on protected actions.
attacks.analogy: A venue that hands out numbered wristbands that increase by one, so you can guess the VIP band number.

mitre.name: Valid Accounts
mitre.note: Using authentication weaknesses to gain valid sessions.

flow.title: Probe
flow.text: Login, reset, and session behavior is examined.

flow.title: Bypass
flow.text: A weak check is abused to obtain or keep a session.

flow.title: Act
flow.text: The attacker uses the account as if they were the user.

caseStudy.title: Session fixation incidents
caseStudy.summary: Applications that accept a pre-set session identifier allow an attacker to reuse a victim's session.
caseStudy.impact: Account takeover without password knowledge.
caseStudy.lesson: Rotate session IDs on login and set secure cookie attributes.

indicators: Password reset tokens that never expire

prevention: Rate limiting and lockout with care

cheatSheet.quick: Rotate IDs, protect cookies, expire tokens, add MFA.

variants.name: Session hijacking
variants.text: Stealing or predicting a session token.

variants.name: IDOR
variants.text: Changing an object ID to access another user's data.

quiz.q: Which cookie attribute prevents JavaScript from reading a session cookie?
quiz.explain: HttpOnly blocks script access; Secure restricts transport, SameSite restricts cross-site sending.

attacks.name: MFA Fatigue
attacks.summary: Repeated MFA push prompts are used to wear down a user until they approve one.
attacks.definition: MFA fatigue (push bombing) abuses push-based multi-factor authentication: an attacker with a valid password triggers many approval requests, hoping the user accepts one out of annoyance or confusion.
attacks.analogy: Someone rings your doorbell every two minutes until you finally open it just to make the noise stop.

mitre.name: Impair Defenses
mitre.note: Abusing the MFA user experience.

flow.title: Have password
flow.text: The attacker already has a valid password from phishing or a leak.

flow.title: Flood
flow.text: Push requests repeat, often late at night.

flow.title: Approve
flow.text: The user accepts to stop the prompts; the attacker gains a session.

caseStudy.title: Uber 2022 incident (reported)
caseStudy.summary: Reports described repeated MFA prompts preceding an account compromise.
caseStudy.impact: Renewed industry push for number matching and phishing-resistant MFA.
caseStudy.lesson: MFA design must consider human factors, not only cryptography.

prevention: User education: deny and report unexpected prompts

tools.examples: Entra ID, Okta, Duo with number matching

cheatSheet.quick: Unexpected prompt? Deny it and report. Never approve to make noise stop.

quiz.q: What should you do with an unexpected MFA prompt?
quiz.explain: Denying and reporting stops the attack and alerts defenders.

attacks.name: Business Email Compromise
attacks.summary: A trusted identity is impersonated to redirect payments or sensitive data.
attacks.definition: BEC uses a compromised or spoofed business email account to convince staff to transfer money or disclose data. It relies on authority, routine, and trust rather than malware.
attacks.analogy: A letter on official letterhead from your 'boss' asking finance to change the landlord's bank account — the paper looks right, but the instruction is a fraud.

mitre.name: Spearphishing via Service
mitre.note: Trusted channels used for deception.

flow.title: Study
flow.text: The attacker learns reporting lines, vendors, and payment cycles.

flow.title: Impersonate
flow.text: An email appears to come from an executive or supplier.

flow.title: Request
flow.text: A plausible, urgent payment change is requested.

flow.title: Transfer
flow.text: Funds are sent to an attacker-controlled account.

caseStudy.title: Global BEC losses
caseStudy.summary: BEC schemes have caused billions of dollars in reported losses worldwide.
caseStudy.impact: Direct financial loss and operational disruption.
caseStudy.lesson: Verification workflows beat visual suspicion.

cheatSheet.quick: Verify every payment change on a known channel, with two people.

variants.name: Invoice fraud
variants.text: Fake or altered invoices.

variants.name: Executive impersonation
variants.text: Authority-based requests.

quiz.q: What is the strongest control against payment redirection fraud?
options: Callback verification using a known number plus dual approval
quiz.explain: Independent verification and separation of duties break the fraud chain.

attacks.name: Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)
attacks.summary: An attacker silently relays or alters communication between two parties.
attacks.definition: A MITM attack places the attacker in the communication path, allowing them to observe, redirect, or modify traffic. Common settings include hostile Wi-Fi, compromised routers, and manipulated DNS or ARP resolution.
attacks.analogy: A postal worker who secretly opens your letters, copies them, sometimes changes a line, and reseals them before delivery.

mitre.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
mitre.note: Interception via network position.

flow.title: Position
flow.text: The attacker gains a path through ARP/DNS spoofing or a fake AP.

flow.title: Relay
flow.text: Traffic flows through the attacker, who forwards it to avoid detection.

flow.title: Abuse
flow.text: Credentials and tokens are captured or responses altered.

caseStudy.title: Public Wi-Fi interception campaigns
caseStudy.summary: Rogue hotspots have been used to capture logins from unsuspecting users.
caseStudy.impact: Account compromise and fraud.
caseStudy.lesson: End-to-end encryption and certificate validation are decisive.

cheatSheet.quick: Encrypt end to end, validate certificates, and distrust unknown networks.

variants.name: ARP poisoning
variants.text: Spoofed ARP replies redirect local traffic.

variants.name: DNS spoofing
variants.text: Name resolution is poisoned.

quiz.q: What does an HTTPS certificate warning indicate?
options: The identity could not be verified — do not proceed
quiz.explain: Warnings mean the chain of trust failed; continuing can expose data to an interceptor.

attacks.name: IoT Botnet
attacks.summary: Large numbers of compromised smart devices used as a remote-controlled army.
attacks.definition: An IoT botnet is a network of compromised cameras, routers, sensors, and other connected devices controlled by an attacker, commonly used for DDoS, spam, or credential attacks.
attacks.analogy: Thousands of household appliances secretly taking orders from one remote conductor.

mitre.name: Network Denial of Service
mitre.note: Botnet used for volumetric attacks.

flow.title: Scan
flow.text: Internet-facing devices with defaults or old firmware are found.

flow.title: Enroll
flow.text: Devices are compromised and join the botnet.

flow.title: Act
flow.text: The controller directs traffic or credential attempts.

caseStudy.title: Mirai (2016)
caseStudy.summary: Mirai scanned for IoT devices with factory-default credentials and built a massive botnet.
caseStudy.impact: Record-breaking DDoS attacks and widespread disruption.
caseStudy.lesson: Change defaults, disable unused services, and keep firmware current.

cheatSheet.quick: No defaults, no exposed management, no flat network.

quiz.q: Why segment IoT devices?
options: To limit spread and outbound traffic if compromised
quiz.explain: Segmentation contains compromise and makes anomalies easier to spot.

attacks.name: Lateral Movement
attacks.summary: Moving from one compromised system to others using legitimate access.
attacks.definition: Lateral movement is the set of techniques attackers use to expand from an initial foothold deeper into a network, often by reusing credentials, remote management tools, or trust relationships already present in the environment.
attacks.analogy: Entering through an unlocked side door, then using keys found inside to open one office after another.

mitre.name: Remote Services
mitre.note: Legitimate remote protocols used for movement.

flow.title: Harvest
flow.text: Credentials, tokens, and host information are collected.

flow.title: Move
flow.text: Remote services are used to access another system.

flow.title: Repeat
flow.text: The process continues toward valuable assets.

caseStudy.title: Colonial Pipeline (2021)
caseStudy.summary: A compromised VPN credential preceded ransomware deployment and operational shutdown.
caseStudy.impact: Fuel supply disruption across the US East Coast.
caseStudy.lesson: Strong remote access controls and network segmentation limit blast radius.

prevention: Local admin password rotation and LAPS

cheatSheet.quick: Break trust paths: MFA, segmentation, unique local admin passwords, behavior detection.

quiz.q: Which control limits reuse of a local admin password across machines?
quiz.explain: Unique credentials stop one compromise from unlocking every machine.

attacks.name: Spear Phishing
attacks.summary: A personalized deceptive message aimed at one person or a small group.
attacks.definition: Spear phishing is phishing researched against a specific target. The attacker uses real names, roles, projects, and relationships to make the message feel routine and trustworthy.
attacks.analogy: A generic scam letter is like junk mail addressed to 'resident'. A spear-phishing letter knows your manager's name, your recent project, and the software your team uses.

mitre.name: Spearphishing Link
mitre.note: A tailored link leads to a fake login.

flow.title: Research
flow.text: Public profiles, org charts, and leaked data provide personal context.

flow.title: Tailor
flow.text: A believable pretext is written using that context.

flow.title: Deliver
flow.text: The message arrives at just the right moment.

flow.title: Exploit
flow.text: The target clicks, reveals data, or approves a request.

caseStudy.title: RSA recruitment attachment
caseStudy.summary: A small group received a tailored email with a spreadsheet named after a recruitment plan.
caseStudy.impact: One opened attachment created the foothold for a major breach.
caseStudy.lesson: Personalization defeats generic filters; verification must be procedural.

indicators: A request that skips normal approval
New sender domain or reply-to mismatch
Attachment from a known contact with unusual context

cheatSheet.quick: Personal does not mean legitimate. Verify the request, not the detail.

variants.name: Whaling
variants.text: Aimed at senior leaders.

variants.name: Smishing
variants.text: Targeted via SMS.

quiz.q: Why is spear phishing harder to spot than bulk phishing?
quiz.explain: Real detail lowers suspicion, so procedural verification matters more than spotting typos.

attacks.name: Vishing
attacks.summary: A phone call used to impersonate a trusted organization and extract secrets or money.
attacks.definition: Vishing is phishing over the phone. Callers use authority, urgency, and helpfulness to convince people to reveal credentials, MFA codes, or make payments.
attacks.analogy: A person wearing a fake uniform knocking on your door and asking to 'check your account' — the costume is the voice and the script.

mitre.name: Spearphishing Voice
mitre.note: Deception delivered by phone.

flow.title: Spoof
flow.text: Caller ID or an AI voice suggests a trusted source.

flow.title: Pretext
flow.text: A problem or deadline is invented.

flow.title: Extract
flow.text: The victim is asked for codes, passwords, or payment.

caseStudy.title: Bank impersonation calls
caseStudy.summary: Callers claim fraud on an account and offer to 'protect' funds by moving them.
caseStudy.impact: Direct financial loss, especially among older adults.
caseStudy.lesson: Hang up and call the number on your card or statement.

indicators: Request for MFA codes or passwords
Pressure to stay on the line

prevention: Call back using a known number
Agree on a family code phrase

cheatSheet.quick: Hang up. Call back on a number you already trust.

variants.name: AI voice clone
variants.text: A synthesized voice imitates a known person.

quiz.q: A caller says they are from your bank and asks for the six-digit code just sent to you. What should you do?
options: Hang up and call the bank's published number
Give only the first three digits
Stay on the line while you check
quiz.explain: One-time codes are meant only for a login you initiated, never for a caller.

attacks.name: Smishing
attacks.summary: Phishing delivered through text messages, often with a link or small payment request.
attacks.definition: Smishing uses SMS or messaging apps to create urgency and direct the victim to a fake site or payment page. Short messages and mobile browsers make careful inspection harder.
attacks.analogy: A note slipped under your door claiming the delivery company needs a tiny fee — just enough to make you pay without thinking.

mitre.name: Phishing via mobile
mitre.note: Mobile message lures.

flow.title: Text
flow.text: A delivery, tax, or bank alert arrives.

flow.title: Tap
flow.text: A shortened link opens a look-alike page.

flow.title: Pay
flow.text: Card details or credentials are captured.

caseStudy.title: Parcel redelivery scams
caseStudy.summary: Texts claim a package cannot be delivered and request a small redelivery fee.
caseStudy.impact: Card theft at enormous scale.
caseStudy.lesson: Open the courier's own app instead of tapping the link.

prevention: Do not tap links in unexpected texts

cheatSheet.quick: Never pay or sign in from a text link.

quiz.q: What is the safest response to a parcel text asking for a small fee?
quiz.explain: Use the channel you already trust rather than a link from an unknown sender.

attacks.name: Pretexting
attacks.summary: An attacker invents a believable situation to build trust and obtain information.
attacks.definition: Pretexting is a longer-form social engineering technique where the attacker adopts a role, such as an auditor or IT contractor, and builds a story that makes requests seem normal.
attacks.analogy: An actor stays in character for weeks, slowly collecting keys because everyone believes they belong there.

mitre.name: Gather Victim Identity Information
mitre.note: Information collected under a false pretext.

flow.title: Role
flow.text: A plausible identity and purpose are chosen.

flow.title: Build
flow.text: Several low-risk interactions establish credibility.

flow.title: Ask
flow.text: A sensitive request is made once trust exists.

caseStudy.title: Fake IT contractor calls
caseStudy.summary: Attackers posing as helpdesk staff have convinced employees to reset passwords or install remote tools.
caseStudy.impact: Account takeover and malware installation.
caseStudy.lesson: Verify identity through an independent directory, not the caller's story.

indicators: Unknown person with detailed internal knowledge

prevention: No secrets over phone or chat

cheatSheet.quick: A good story is not proof of identity.

quiz.q: What is the key defense against pretexting?
quiz.explain: Verify who someone is through a channel or directory you already trust.

attacks.name: Baiting
attacks.summary: Offering something tempting to trick a person into an unsafe action.
attacks.definition: Baiting uses curiosity or greed as the hook: a free download, a lost USB drive, or an irresistible offer that leads to malware or credential theft.
attacks.analogy: A shiny wallet left on a bench with a note saying 'free gift inside' — the object itself is the trap.

mitre.name: Hardware Additions
mitre.note: Malicious device introduced into the environment.

flow.title: Lure
flow.text: An attractive item or offer appears.

flow.title: Take
flow.text: The victim plugs in, downloads, or signs up.

flow.title: Hook
flow.text: Malware runs or credentials are stolen.

caseStudy.title: Dropped USB drives
caseStudy.summary: Studies show a surprising number of people plug unknown USB drives into work computers.
caseStudy.impact: Malware execution or data theft.
caseStudy.lesson: Treat unknown media as hazardous waste, not a finders-keep prize.

cheatSheet.quick: If you did not ask for it, do not plug it in or download it.

quiz.q: What should you do with an unknown USB drive found in the office?
options: Plug it in to identify the owner
Hand it to security without using it
quiz.explain: Unknown media can execute code or steal data; security can handle it safely.

attacks.name: Trojan Horse
attacks.summary: Malware disguised as something useful or harmless.
attacks.definition: A trojan presents itself as a legitimate program — a game, utility, or document — while secretly performing malicious actions once installed.
attacks.analogy: A wooden horse wheeled into the city as a gift, with soldiers hidden inside.

mitre.name: Malicious File
mitre.note: User execution of a disguised file.

flow.title: Disguise
flow.text: Malware is packaged as an attractive or useful file.

flow.title: Install
flow.text: The user runs it voluntarily.

flow.title: Act
flow.text: Hidden functionality steals data or opens a backdoor.

caseStudy.title: Fake utility installers
caseStudy.summary: Search ads have led users to convincing fake installers bundled with information stealers.
caseStudy.impact: Credential theft and follow-on fraud.
caseStudy.lesson: Download from official sources and verify signatures.

cheatSheet.quick: The label is a costume; check the source and signature.

variants.name: Information stealer
variants.text: Focused on cookies and credentials.

variants.name: Remote access trojan
variants.text: Gives attackers interactive control.

quiz.q: What makes a trojan different from a worm?
options: It relies on a user to install it
quiz.explain: Trojans rely on disguise and user execution; worms self-propagate.

attacks.name: Worm
attacks.summary: Malware that copies itself to other systems without user action.
attacks.definition: A worm spreads automatically by exploiting vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, or trusted relationships. Its defining feature is self-propagation.
attacks.analogy: A rumor that every person who hears it immediately tells everyone else, with no encouragement needed.

mitre.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
mitre.note: Automated spread via a flaw.

flow.title: Scan
flow.text: The worm looks for reachable vulnerable hosts.

flow.title: Exploit
flow.text: A flaw or weak credential allows entry.

flow.title: Copy
flow.text: The worm installs itself and repeats.

caseStudy.title: WannaCry
caseStudy.summary: A wormable strain spread via an SMB vulnerability across unpatched systems.
caseStudy.impact: Global disruption in hospitals and industry.
caseStudy.lesson: Patch speed and disabling obsolete protocols stop spread.

cheatSheet.quick: Stop the scan, patch the flaw, segment the network.

quiz.q: What best limits a worm's spread?
quiz.explain: Removing the flaw and containing the network path stops propagation.

attacks.name: Spyware
attacks.summary: Software that secretly observes activity and sends data to another party.
attacks.definition: Spyware monitors keystrokes, screenshots, browsing, or location without meaningful consent. It is often bundled with free software or installed by someone with physical access.
attacks.analogy: A hidden camera and microphone in your own room, quietly recording everything and posting it elsewhere.

mitre.name: Input Capture
mitre.note: Keystrokes and screen content collected.

flow.title: Install
flow.text: Spyware arrives via a bundle or physical access.

flow.title: Observe
flow.text: Input, location, or files are recorded.

flow.title: Send
flow.text: Data is transmitted to the operator.

caseStudy.title: Stalkerware apps
caseStudy.summary: Commercial apps have been used to monitor partners and employees without consent.
caseStudy.impact: Privacy violations and physical safety risks.
caseStudy.lesson: Check installed apps and device profiles; seek help safely if abuse is suspected.

response: Rotate credentials from a clean device
Seek support if safety is a concern

cheatSheet.quick: Unknown apps plus odd permissions equals investigate.

quiz.q: Which permission is a strong spyware signal on a phone?
quiz.explain: These powerful permissions can read screens and control the device.

attacks.name: Rootkit
attacks.summary: Malware that hides its own presence by subverting the operating system.
attacks.definition: A rootkit uses privileged access to conceal processes, files, or network connections. The name comes from 'root' level access and the 'kit' of hiding tools.
attacks.analogy: A burglar who repaints the security camera's view so it always shows an empty room.

mitre.name: Rootkit
mitre.note: Concealment using privileged components.

flow.title: Privilege
flow.text: The attacker gains high-level access.

flow.title: Hook
flow.text: System functions are altered to hide artifacts.

flow.title: Persist
flow.text: The implant survives reboots and hides in plain sight.

caseStudy.title: Kernel rootkit campaigns
caseStudy.summary: Advanced actors used signed or kernel-level components to hide long-term access.
caseStudy.impact: Difficult detection and prolonged intrusions.
caseStudy.lesson: Trusted boot, driver signing, and out-of-band telemetry matter.

response: Rotate all credentials on the host

cheatSheet.quick: Do not trust a compromised host to report on itself.

quiz.q: What is the defining feature of a rootkit?
options: It hides its presence using privileged access
quiz.explain: Concealment at a privileged level is what makes rootkits hard to detect.

attacks.name: Fileless Malware
attacks.summary: Malicious activity that runs in memory or through legitimate system tools.
attacks.definition: Fileless techniques avoid writing traditional executable files. They use scripts, macros, or trusted administrative tools already present on the system, which makes signature detection harder.
attacks.analogy: Instead of bringing a weapon, the intruder uses the tools already in the building — the ladder, the keys, the phone.

mitre.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
mitre.note: Legitimate interpreters abused for execution.

flow.title: Enter
flow.text: A script, document macro, or stolen session starts the activity.

flow.title: Execute
flow.text: PowerShell, WMI, or similar tools run commands in memory.

flow.title: Blend
flow.text: Activity looks like normal administration.

caseStudy.title: PowerShell-based intrusions
caseStudy.summary: Attackers frequently use built-in scripting engines to download payloads and move laterally.
caseStudy.impact: Low signature footprint and long dwell time.
caseStudy.lesson: Behavioral detection and script logging are essential.

cheatSheet.quick: Watch behavior, not just files.

quiz.q: Why is fileless malware harder to detect with antivirus signatures?
options: It often uses legitimate tools already on the system
quiz.explain: Using trusted system tools makes malicious behavior look like normal administration.

attacks.name: DNS Spoofing
attacks.summary: Corrupting name resolution so a trusted domain points to an attacker-controlled address.
attacks.definition: DNS spoofing inserts false DNS answers into a resolver's cache or a victim's host file, causing a legitimate-looking hostname to resolve to the wrong IP address.
attacks.analogy: Changing the entries in a city's address book so the bank's name points to a shop run by a scammer.

mitre.name: Compromise DNS
mitre.note: Infrastructure manipulated for redirection.

flow.title: Target
flow.text: A resolver or host's DNS settings are chosen.

flow.title: Poison
flow.text: False records are injected or cached.

flow.title: Redirect
flow.text: Users reach a fake site with a familiar name.

caseStudy.title: DNS cache poisoning incidents
caseStudy.summary: Research demonstrated that predictable transaction IDs could allow cache poisoning.
caseStudy.impact: Users could be redirected to malicious sites without any visible warning.
caseStudy.lesson: Randomization, DNSSEC, and encrypted DNS reduce risk.

cheatSheet.quick: Trust the certificate, not just the hostname.

quiz.q: What does DNSSEC help validate?
quiz.explain: DNSSEC signs DNS records so resolvers can reject forged answers.

attacks.name: ARP Poisoning
attacks.summary: Spoofed local network messages redirect traffic through an attacker's machine.
attacks.definition: ARP poisoning sends forged Address Resolution Protocol replies so devices associate an IP address with the attacker's MAC address, enabling interception on a local network.
attacks.analogy: Convincing everyone in an office that the mailroom is now the desk next to the elevator, so all parcels are handed to the wrong person first.

mitre.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
mitre.note: Local traffic interception.

flow.title: Scan
flow.text: The attacker maps local IP and MAC addresses.

flow.title: Spoof
flow.text: Forged ARP replies poison caches.

flow.title: Relay
flow.text: Traffic flows through the attacker and is forwarded.

caseStudy.title: Campus network interception
caseStudy.summary: Students have demonstrated ARP spoofing on shared networks to capture unencrypted logins.
caseStudy.impact: Credential exposure on flat networks.
caseStudy.lesson: Dynamic ARP inspection and encryption remove the opportunity.

cheatSheet.quick: Fix the mapping and encrypt the traffic.

quiz.q: Which switch feature directly counters ARP spoofing?
quiz.explain: DAI validates ARP messages against trusted DHCP bindings.

attacks.name: Port Scanning
attacks.summary: Systematically checking which network ports and services are exposed.
attacks.definition: Port scanning sends connection attempts to a range of ports to learn what services are listening. It is a reconnaissance technique — not an attack by itself, but often the first step toward one.
attacks.analogy: Walking along a building and quietly noting which doors are unlocked and which windows are open.

mitre.name: Network Service Discovery
mitre.note: Reconnaissance of listening services.

flow.title: Sweep
flow.text: Many ports are probed quickly.

flow.title: Identify
flow.text: Responses reveal services and versions.

flow.title: Plan
flow.text: The attacker chooses a likely weakness to pursue.

caseStudy.title: Internet-wide scanning
caseStudy.summary: Automated scanners continuously map exposed services across the internet.
caseStudy.impact: Newly exposed devices are found within minutes.
caseStudy.lesson: Minimize exposed ports and monitor unsolicited connection attempts.

indicators: Many connection attempts from one IP

cheatSheet.quick: Reduce what is visible and watch who is looking.

quiz.q: Is port scanning itself an attack?
options: It is reconnaissance; intent and authorization matter
quiz.explain: Scanning maps exposure; it becomes unauthorized activity when performed without permission.

attacks.name: CSRF
attacks.summary: Tricking a logged-in user's browser into performing an action they did not intend.
attacks.definition: CSRF abuses the fact that browsers automatically attach cookies to requests. A malicious page can cause a signed-in user's browser to submit a request to another site, which the server treats as authentic.
attacks.analogy: Someone uses your already-open elevator keycard to enter a room you did not mean to enter — the card is valid, but the visit is not yours.

mitre.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
mitre.note: Abuse of a web trust relationship.

flow.title: Lure
flow.text: A logged-in user visits a malicious page.

flow.title: Forge
flow.text: The page silently sends a request to the target site.

flow.title: Act
flow.text: The server performs the action using the user's session.

caseStudy.title: Router CSRF incidents
caseStudy.summary: Home router admin pages were abused via crafted links that changed DNS settings.
caseStudy.impact: Users were redirected to malicious sites.
caseStudy.lesson: State-changing actions need unpredictable tokens, not just cookies.

cheatSheet.quick: Make every state change carry a secret the attacker cannot guess.

quiz.q: What does a SameSite cookie help prevent?
quiz.explain: SameSite limits when cookies are sent with cross-site requests.

attacks.name: SSRF
attacks.summary: Tricking a server into making requests to places it should not reach.
attacks.definition: SSRF occurs when an application fetches a URL supplied by a user without validating the destination. The attacker can make the server connect to internal services or cloud metadata endpoints.
attacks.analogy: Convincing a trusted office assistant to fetch a document from any address you name — including the locked filing cabinet they normally cannot access.

mitre.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
mitre.note: Abuse of server-side request functionality.

flow.title: Find
flow.text: A URL-fetching feature is identified.

flow.title: Point
flow.text: The attacker supplies an internal or restricted target.

flow.title: Read
flow.text: The server returns data from a trusted position.

caseStudy.title: Cloud metadata exposure
caseStudy.summary: SSRF has been used to reach cloud instance metadata and obtain temporary credentials.
caseStudy.impact: Privilege escalation and data access.
caseStudy.lesson: Enforce allow-lists and require IMDSv2-style protections.

cheatSheet.quick: Never let user input choose where the server connects.

quiz.q: What is the core defense against SSRF?
quiz.explain: The server must only be allowed to fetch trusted, expected destinations.

attacks.name: IDOR
attacks.summary: Changing an identifier in a request to access someone else's data.
attacks.definition: IDOR happens when an application exposes a direct reference to an object — such as a numeric record ID — without checking whether the current user is allowed to see it.
attacks.analogy: A hotel gives you a key numbered 214, and you notice that changing the number to 213 opens another guest's room.

mitre.name: Valid Accounts
mitre.note: Authorized access used beyond its scope.

flow.title: Observe
flow.text: A predictable identifier appears in a URL or API call.

flow.title: Change
flow.text: The attacker tries a different identifier.

flow.title: Access
flow.text: Another user's record is returned.

caseStudy.title: API enumeration incidents
caseStudy.summary: Many public bug reports describe sequential IDs exposing private documents or invoices.
caseStudy.impact: Large-scale data exposure without malware.
caseStudy.lesson: Authorization must be checked on every object, every time.

cheatSheet.quick: Never trust an ID just because the user is logged in.

quiz.q: What prevents IDOR most reliably?
options: Authorization checks on every object request
quiz.explain: Obfuscation is not access control; each request must be authorized.

attacks.name: OWASP Top 10
attacks.summary: A regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks.
attacks.definition: The OWASP Top 10 is a consensus reference for web risks such as broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, and insecure design. It is a prioritization aid, not a complete standard.
attacks.analogy: A fire department's list of the ten most common causes of house fires — useful for where to focus inspections, but not the whole of fire safety.

mitre.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
mitre.note: Many web risks lead to initial access.

flow.title: Map
flow.text: Identify which categories apply to your application.

flow.title: Test
flow.text: Use authorized testing to confirm exposure.

flow.title: Fix
flow.text: Prioritize by real risk and business context.

caseStudy.title: A decade of web breaches
caseStudy.summary: Injection and access-control failures have repeatedly appeared in major incidents.
caseStudy.impact: Data theft and account takeover at scale.
caseStudy.lesson: Secure design and testing shift fixes left, before production.

cheatSheet.quick: Use the list to prioritize, then test and fix what actually applies.

quiz.q: What is the OWASP Top 10 best used for?
options: As a starting point for prioritizing web risks
quiz.explain: It is a widely used awareness and prioritization reference, not an exhaustive standard.

attacks.name: Rogue Access Point
attacks.summary: An unauthorized wireless access point connected to a network or mimicking a trusted one.
attacks.definition: A rogue access point is a Wi-Fi device installed without approval. It may be a misconfigured employee router or a deliberate device used to intercept traffic and bypass network controls.
attacks.analogy: Someone puts an extra, unmonitored door on the side of a secure building and invites everyone to use it.

mitre.name: Compromise Infrastructure: Access Point
mitre.note: Unauthorized network entry point.

flow.title: Add
flow.text: An AP appears without authorization.

flow.title: Connect
flow.text: Users join it, believing it is legitimate.

flow.title: Bypass
flow.text: Traffic or access avoids normal controls.

caseStudy.title: Employee hotspot incidents
caseStudy.summary: Convenient consumer routers have created unsecured bridges into corporate networks.
caseStudy.impact: Bypassed segmentation and exposed credentials.
caseStudy.lesson: Wireless IDS and port controls catch what policy alone misses.

cheatSheet.quick: If it broadcasts, inventory it.

quiz.q: Which control best prevents an employee from adding an unauthorized AP?
quiz.explain: Identity-based network access and port control stop unapproved devices from joining.

attacks.name: Bluetooth Attack
attacks.summary: Abusing Bluetooth pairing or proximity features to access devices or data.
attacks.definition: Bluetooth attacks exploit weak pairing, discoverable devices, or insecure profiles. They require proximity, which limits scale but makes public places a realistic setting.
attacks.analogy: A stranger striking up a conversation at arm's length and talking you into handing over your address book.

mitre.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
mitre.note: Short-range interception.

flow.title: Discover
flow.text: Discoverable devices are found nearby.

flow.title: Pair
flow.text: A weak or deceptive pairing is accepted.

flow.title: Access
flow.text: Data or device functions are abused.

caseStudy.title: BlueBorne vulnerabilities
caseStudy.summary: Flaws in Bluetooth stacks exposed many devices to proximity-based compromise.
caseStudy.impact: Wide patching effort across phones and laptops.
caseStudy.lesson: Keep operating systems updated and turn Bluetooth off when unused.

cheatSheet.quick: Proximity is not permission. Reject unknown pairings.

quiz.q: What reduces Bluetooth attack exposure most?
options: Updating the OS and disabling Bluetooth when unused
quiz.explain: Patches fix stack flaws and turning it off removes the attack surface.

attacks.name: Cloud Privilege Escalation
attacks.summary: Turning limited cloud permissions into broader access than intended.
attacks.definition: Cloud privilege escalation exploits overly permissive roles, role-chaining, or misconfigured services so an identity can obtain permissions it was not meant to have.
attacks.analogy: A library volunteer badge that, due to a paperwork error, also opens the archive and the manager's office.

mitre.name: Account Manipulation
mitre.note: Permissions and roles altered for broader access.

flow.title: Inspect
flow.text: The attacker maps IAM policies and trust relationships.

flow.title: Chain
flow.text: A permissive role or service is used to gain more rights.

flow.title: Expand
flow.text: New keys or roles are created for persistence.

caseStudy.title: Over-permissive cloud roles
caseStudy.summary: Attackers regularly abuse wildcard IAM statements after phishing a developer account.
caseStudy.impact: Full account compromise and data theft.
caseStudy.lesson: Least privilege and periodic access reviews are non-negotiable.

cheatSheet.quick: Assume every identity will be tested; keep permissions tiny.

quiz.q: Which IAM practice best limits escalation?
options: Static keys shared by the team
quiz.explain: Minimal, reviewed permissions shrink both accidental and malicious reach.

attacks.name: Insecure API
attacks.summary: An application programming interface that exposes data or actions without adequate checks.
attacks.definition: Insecure APIs suffer from missing authentication, weak authorization, excessive data exposure, or missing rate limits. Because APIs are machine-facing, flaws often scale quickly.
attacks.analogy: A self-service counter with no attendant, where anyone can ask for anyone else's file and the shelf simply hands it over.

mitre.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
mitre.note: API abuse for access.

flow.title: Discover
flow.text: Endpoints are enumerated from apps or docs.

flow.title: Probe
flow.text: Missing checks are tested.

flow.title: Abuse
flow.text: Data or functions are accessed at scale.

caseStudy.title: Exposed social API
caseStudy.summary: A social platform API allowed mass phone-number lookups because rate and authorization checks were weak.
caseStudy.impact: Hundreds of millions of profiles scraped.
caseStudy.lesson: APIs need the same rigor as user interfaces, plus rate limiting.

cheatSheet.quick: Authenticate, authorize, validate, and rate-limit every endpoint.

quiz.q: Why are APIs attractive targets?
options: They expose structured data and actions at machine speed
quiz.explain: Machine-speed access turns a small flaw into a large exposure quickly.

attacks.name: Credential Leak
attacks.summary: Passwords, tokens, or keys exposed in code, logs, or configuration.
attacks.definition: Credential leaks happen when secrets are committed to repositories, written to logs, pasted into tickets, or stored in front-end code. Attackers scan continuously for these mistakes.
attacks.analogy: Writing your safe combination on the outside of the safe and leaving it in the lobby.

mitre.name: Credentials in Files
mitre.note: Secrets discovered in configuration or code.

flow.title: Expose
flow.text: A secret is published accidentally.

flow.title: Discover
flow.text: Automated scanners find it.

flow.title: Use
flow.text: The attacker authenticates as the service.

caseStudy.title: Public repository keys
caseStudy.summary: Cloud keys pushed to public repositories are often abused within minutes.
caseStudy.impact: Cryptomining, data theft, and large bills.
caseStudy.lesson: Use secret scanning and short-lived credentials everywhere.

prevention: Never ship secrets to the browser

cheatSheet.quick: Rotate first, investigate second.

quiz.q: What is the first action after discovering a leaked cloud key?
options: Wait to see if it is used
quiz.explain: Revocation ends misuse; investigation comes after containment.

attacks.name: Password Spraying
attacks.summary: Trying a small set of common passwords against many accounts to avoid lockouts.
attacks.definition: Password spraying reverses brute force: instead of many guesses on one account, an attacker tries one or two common passwords across thousands of accounts, staying below lockout thresholds.
attacks.analogy: Trying the same handful of keys on every door in a building rather than jamming one lock.

mitre.name: Password Spraying
mitre.note: Avoids account lockout by spreading attempts.

flow.title: List
flow.text: A list of usernames is gathered.

flow.title: Spray
flow.text: A common password is tried across many accounts.

flow.title: Win
flow.text: Any match becomes a foothold.

caseStudy.title: Corporate VPN spraying
caseStudy.summary: Remote-access portals are routinely targeted with seasonal or default passwords.
caseStudy.impact: Initial access leading to ransomware in some cases.
caseStudy.lesson: MFA and breach-password screening break the pattern.

indicators: Many accounts with one failed login each

cheatSheet.quick: Watch the pattern across accounts, not just one user.

quiz.q: How does password spraying avoid lockouts?
options: By spreading few guesses across many accounts
quiz.explain: Low per-account volume keeps attempts below typical thresholds.

attacks.name: Brute Force
attacks.summary: Trying many password possibilities until one works.
attacks.definition: Brute force attempts a large number of guesses against an account or encrypted data. It is slowed by rate limits, lockouts, and strong passwords, but remains common against weak or exposed services.
attacks.analogy: Trying every combination on a three-digit luggage lock until it clicks open.

mitre.name: Password Guessing
mitre.note: Repeated authentication attempts.

flow.title: Choose
flow.text: A target and word list are selected.

flow.title: Guess
flow.text: Many attempts are made quickly.

flow.title: Match
flow.text: A valid password grants access.

caseStudy.title: Exposed SSH services
caseStudy.summary: Internet-facing SSH endpoints receive constant automated guessing attempts.
caseStudy.impact: Compromise of weak accounts.
caseStudy.lesson: Disable password login, use keys and MFA, and rate-limit.

cheatSheet.quick: Make guessing slow and expensive.

quiz.q: Which control most directly slows brute force?
quiz.explain: Limits on attempts plus a second factor make guessing impractical.

attacks.name: Session Hijacking
attacks.summary: Stealing or predicting a session token to act as a logged-in user.
attacks.definition: Session hijacking takes over an authenticated session by obtaining its cookie or token through interception, malware, XSS, or predictable identifiers. The attacker skips the login step entirely.
attacks.analogy: Stealing a valid backstage pass instead of forging an ID at the front door.

mitre.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
mitre.note: Reuse of a valid session.

flow.title: Obtain
flow.text: A token is captured through a browser or network weakness.

flow.title: Replay
flow.text: The attacker presents the token to the service.

flow.title: Act
flow.text: Actions appear to come from the real user.

caseStudy.title: Cookie theft via infostealers
caseStudy.summary: Malware steals browser cookies to bypass MFA on authenticated sessions.
caseStudy.impact: Account takeover despite strong passwords.
caseStudy.lesson: Bind sessions to devices, shorten lifetimes, and detect reuse.

cheatSheet.quick: A session is a key; revoke it, not just the password.

quiz.q: Why is revoking sessions important after a suspected theft?
options: It invalidates the stolen token immediately
quiz.explain: A password change alone may not invalidate an already active session.

attacks.name: Physical Security Breach
attacks.summary: Physical access or observation used to bypass digital controls.
attacks.definition: Physical security threats include tailgating through doors, shoulder-surfing screens, stealing badges, or accessing unattended devices. Digital controls cannot help if someone can simply sit down at a logged-in workstation.
attacks.analogy: A high-tech lock on the front door, but the side door is held open by someone carrying a stack of boxes.

mitre.name: Hardware Additions
mitre.note: Physical access enables device tampering.

flow.title: Observe
flow.text: Badges, screens, and routines are noted.

flow.title: Enter
flow.text: Access is gained by following or borrowing trust.

flow.title: Act
flow.text: Devices or documents are accessed.

caseStudy.title: Shoulder-surfing in public
caseStudy.summary: Observing passwords or MFA codes in trains and cafes is a simple, effective technique.
caseStudy.impact: Account compromise without any technical exploit.
caseStudy.lesson: Use privacy screens and be aware of surroundings.

cheatSheet.quick: Lock it, challenge it, escort it.

variants.name: Piggybacking
variants.text: Following someone through a door with permission.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see someone you do not recognize in a secure area?
options: Take a photo for social media
quiz.explain: Challenge respectfully or report according to policy.

attacks.name: Zero-Day Exploit
attacks.summary: Attacking a vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor and has no patch.
attacks.definition: A zero-day is a flaw unknown to the software maker, so defenders have had zero days to prepare. Once discovered and disclosed, it becomes an n-day and can be patched.
attacks.analogy: A lock picking method the lock maker has never seen — until someone uses it, there is no new lock to install.

mitre.name: Exploitation for Client Execution
mitre.note: Unknown flaw used before a patch exists.

flow.title: Discover
flow.text: A previously unknown flaw is found.

flow.title: Use
flow.text: It is used before a vendor fix is available.

flow.title: Disclose
flow.text: Discovery leads to a patch and detection signatures.

caseStudy.title: Stuxnet
caseStudy.summary: Multiple zero-days were combined in a highly targeted operation.
caseStudy.impact: Physical disruption and a new era of sophisticated malware.
caseStudy.lesson: Assume flaws exist; limit exposure and detect behavior, not just signatures.

cheatSheet.quick: You cannot patch what you do not know — reduce surface and watch behavior.

quiz.q: What makes a zero-day especially dangerous?
options: No patch exists when it is first used
quiz.explain: Defenders have no vendor fix yet, so layered controls and behavior detection matter.

attacks.name: Data Exfiltration
attacks.summary: Unauthorized transfer of data out of an organization.
attacks.definition: Exfiltration is the stage where stolen information leaves the victim's control. Attackers use encrypted channels, cloud storage, or slow low-volume transfers to blend into normal traffic.
attacks.analogy: A thief does not run out with a stack of documents; they photocopy a few pages each day and mail them quietly.

mitre.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
mitre.note: Data sent through an existing covert channel.

flow.title: Stage
flow.text: Valuable data is collected into a staging area.

flow.title: Move
flow.text: It leaves via an approved-looking channel.

flow.title: Monetize
flow.text: Data is sold, leaked, or used for further attacks.

caseStudy.title: Double extortion ransomware
caseStudy.summary: Ransomware groups steal data before encrypting systems to increase pressure.
caseStudy.impact: Regulatory fines and reputational damage even after restoration.
caseStudy.lesson: Egress monitoring and DLP are as important as backups.

cheatSheet.quick: Watch the exit, not only the entrance.

quiz.q: Why do attackers exfiltrate slowly?
options: To blend in with normal traffic
quiz.explain: Low-and-slow transfers are less likely to trigger volume alerts.

attacks.name: Prompt Injection
attacks.summary: Hidden instructions in content manipulate an AI assistant's behavior.
attacks.definition: Prompt injection places instructions inside data an AI system reads — a webpage, document, or email — causing it to ignore its real task and follow the attacker's instructions instead.
attacks.analogy: A note hidden in a book that says to the librarian 'ignore the next customer and hand them the wrong file' — the librarian reads it as part of the job.

mitre.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
mitre.note: Manipulating an automated agent's instructions.

flow.title: Hide
flow.text: Instructions are embedded in content the AI will read.

flow.title: Ingest
flow.text: The assistant processes the content as trusted context.

flow.title: Act
flow.text: It follows the injected instruction.

caseStudy.title: Hidden text in web pages
caseStudy.summary: Researchers showed that invisible text on pages could steer AI browsing assistants.
caseStudy.impact: Misleading summaries and unintended actions.
caseStudy.lesson: Treat model output as untrusted and keep humans in the loop.

cheatSheet.quick: Never let content become commands without verification.

quiz.q: What is the safest design for an AI assistant with tool access?
options: Let it act on any instruction it reads
Require human approval for consequential actions
quiz.explain: Keep the agent's power small and require approval for anything that matters.

attacks.name: Deepfake
attacks.summary: AI-generated audio or video that imitates a real person.
attacks.definition: Deepfakes use machine learning to synthesize convincing voice or video. In security, they are used for impersonation fraud, misinformation, and fake evidence.
attacks.analogy: A perfect actor wearing someone else's face and voice — familiar to the eye and ear, but not the person you think you are dealing with.

mitre.name: Phishing
mitre.note: Synthetic identity used for deception.

flow.title: Collect
flow.text: Public voice and video samples are gathered.

flow.title: Generate
flow.text: A synthetic recording or video is produced.

flow.title: Deliver
flow.text: It supports a fraudulent request.

caseStudy.title: Executive voice cloning fraud
caseStudy.summary: Reported cases used cloned voices to authorize urgent transfers.
caseStudy.impact: Financial loss and distrust of familiar media.
caseStudy.lesson: Verification must not depend on voice or face alone.

indicators: Refusal to use a known channel

cheatSheet.quick: Familiar face or voice is not proof. Verify the request.

quiz.q: What is the strongest check on a 'CEO video' requesting a payment?
options: A callback on a saved number
quiz.explain: Independent verification defeats synthetic media.
